\chapter{A finales de año}
\label{ch:es-a-finales-de-ano}
\hlchaptermodality{540}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say whether something happened at the beginning, in the middle or at the end of a month or a year, and how often it happens.}

\section[a principios de]{a principios de — at the beginning of}

\label{lesson:ES-C540-a-principios-de}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the millennium, then the Spanish for the period.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a principios de}
\textbf{a principios de} — \textquotedblleft{}at the beginning of\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Llegaron a principios de junio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They arrived at the beginning of June.}
\end{quote}

Used with months, years and centuries: \emph{a principios del siglo XX}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{a principios de} is built on \emph{principio}, from Latin \emph{prīncipium} 'a beginning' (Lewis \& Short), which comes from \emph{prīnceps} 'first'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a principios de}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a principios de}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a principios de}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the millennium, then the Spanish for the period, then say \emph{a principios de} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a principios de mean? (\textquotedblleft{}At the beginning of\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a mediados de]{a mediados de — in the middle of, around the middle of}

\label{lesson:ES-C540-a-mediados-de}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the period, then the Spanish for at the beginning of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a mediados de}
\textbf{a mediados de} — \textquotedblleft{}in the middle of, around the middle of\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{a mediados de} is built on \emph{mediado}, from \emph{mediar} 'to reach the middle', which comes from Latin \emph{medius} 'middle' (Lewis \& Short).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[a finales de]{a finales de — at the end of}

\label{lesson:ES-C540-a-finales-de}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for at the beginning of, then the Spanish for in the middle of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a finales de}
\textbf{a finales de} — \textquotedblleft{}at the end of\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se jubiló a finales del año pasado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He retired at the end of last year.}
\end{quote}

\emph{A fines de} is also common in Latin America.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{a finales de} is built on \emph{final}, a learned word from Latin \emph{fīnālis}, which comes from \emph{fīnis} 'end, boundary' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a finales de}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a finales de}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for at the beginning of, then the Spanish for in the middle of, then say \emph{a finales de} again

\section[semanal]{semanal — weekly}

\label{lesson:ES-C540-semanal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for in the middle of, then the Spanish for at the end of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: semanal}
\textbf{semanal} — \textquotedblleft{}weekly\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El mercado semanal es los jueves.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The weekly market is on Thursdays.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{semanal} is built on \emph{semana} 'week' with the ending \emph{-al} (EtymDB). \emph{Semana} is inherited from Late Latin \emph{septimāna} 'a set of seven', built on \emph{septem} 'seven'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{semanal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{semanal}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{semanal}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for in the middle of, then the Spanish for at the end of, then say \emph{semanal} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[anual]{anual — yearly, annual}

\label{lesson:ES-C540-anual}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for at the end of, then the Spanish for weekly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: anual}
\textbf{anual} — \textquotedblleft{}yearly, annual\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La fiesta anual del pueblo es en agosto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The town's annual festival is in August.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{anual} is a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{annuālis} 'yearly' (EtymDB), built on \emph{annus} 'year'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\end{itemize}
